newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Prodi says Germany lacks commitment to EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Prodi says Germany lacks commitment to EMU.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Monday accused Germany of lacking political commitment to Europe's single currency, saying that Rome was making more effort to tackle its problems than the Bonn government.

Laying down the law to a German public which is openly sceptical about whether Italy's track record is strong enough to allow it into monetary union, Prodi said Italy, in contrast to Germany, was at least fully in favour of the currency plan.
"We see our future in Europe. I don't know if that is the case in Germany," he told a briefing in Frankfurt.
Falling short of criticising German Chancellor Helmut Kohl by name, Prodi added, "Last year Germany was a model. This year Germany is a disaster...I would expect stronger leadership from Germany."

Earlier, Prodi lashed out at Germany's political leadership for failing to take the action needed to shape up the German economy for a punctual start of monetary union in 1999 by cutting its budget deficits and lowering public debt.
Prodi told Reuters Financial Television, "There is a difference between Italy and Germany. We have economic problems and I have prepared a strategy to solve them."

Germany, posting its highest unemployment level since the 1930s, has run into trouble as the government focuses on saving to meet the political goal of currency union rather than tackling economic problems, like high unemployment.
Long-delayed and much-needed reforms of its tax and pension systems have been proposed, but are still politically deadlocked within the consensus-driven German decision process.
"Germany has more political problems than economic problems," Prodi said, adding, "if Germany wanted it could exercise the political leadership which is needed now."

Prodi travelled to Germany on Monday -- his second visit to the country in 11 days -- for a meeting with Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber in Munich and a dinner with top industrialists and bankers in the financial capital of Frankfurt.
Stoiber has been one of the most vocal politicians in Germany in insisting that the future euro must be rock-solid.
For most Germans, this means excluding countries such as Italy and Spain -- which have been better known for conducting inflationary policies than for their emphasis on stability.
Prodi emphasised his nation would be ready to join Europe's currency union in 1999 and expected to be allowed in.
"It is puzzling to me that every other day some one is authorised to say Italy/Spain should not come in. That is difficult to understand," he said.

This year will be critical for nations wishing to join the currency union in 1999 as it will be their last chance to show that budget deficit and government debt ratios meet the strict Maastricht Treaty entry criteria.

Political leaders will choose the first group of nations to adopt the new currency early next year, and it is largely expected to include Germany along with France, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg as well as a few others.

Senior bankers have recently warned of turmoil in the financial markets if Mediterranean countries like Italy, whose currencies have been less stable than the mark, were allowed to help launch the euro.
But Prodi countered that he was already getting good marks for his policies and his consistency of purpose.

Responding to a question on how his tenure so far would be judged, Prodi said, "Look at my record for the past and my plans for the future. I am organising consistent policies and the markets perceive this."
